results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 33 prose units' summaries match the controlling ideas of their aligned spec paragraphs p01-p33 in spec order; the five introduction callouts are framing apparatus and match no spec paragraph.

Marked two_ideas. The margin sentence is a one-clause reading of the table's margin row that leads into the paragraph's controlling idea (the last row matters most: the group pays several times over); spec p05 frames both as one reading of the glance table. One controlling idea.

results.draft_locus: Volumes Every Design Is Sized Against ¶2
results.finding: Marked two_ideas. The paragraph opens 'Two caveats on reading it.': one controlling idea (how to read the volumes table) with two supporting caveats, as spec p13 declares.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: intro and examples/chapters to MV1, glance/history/systems to MV3, brands and volumes to MV2, problems to MV4, Common Ground to MV5, and the closing synthesizes all five.
Glance table is read by the following paragraph: margin typical of classifieds; last row means capabilities are paid for several times.
Timeline is followed by 'Each phase left a layer in the systems', naming what each phase left.

results.draft_locus: Four Brands, Four Business Models ¶1-¶2 (table, Figure 1)
results.finding: Brand table is summarised by the revenue-share sentence ('none above a third'); Figure 1's caption states the four marketplace physics.
Each portfolio fact is tied to its consequence (never learns whether sold; B2B software; data product; neutrality as a design constraint).

results.draft_locus: Volumes Every Design Is Sized Against ¶1-¶2 (table)
results.finding: Table introduced as what every design is sized against; NL/PT ratio statistic is explained as ratios mattering more than totals, with the liquidity link.
Figure 2 caption and the 'Three facts in this landscape shape most of the book' list explain the systems table; the 214-column ads table fact explains why Yardstick blocks Tradeyard.
Lead-in states the cast table's point: each person owns something and the tensions are between legitimate goals.

results.draft_locus: Eight Problems Veldmark Starts 2027 With ¶1-¶2 (list, Figure 3)
results.finding: Each problem carries its pattern; Figure 3 caption states 'four of everything'; ¶2 reads the list (none is a technology problem alone).
Three shared-but-local examples illustrate the principle; Figure 4 caption restates what brands keep and what Common Ground builds.
Decision table names the chapter that works each decision and is followed by Figure 5's caption explaining the four plateaus; the lead-in's ordering problem is recorded under flow_is_followable.

Table introduced as fixed facts to follow across chapters; the bike scenario ends with what it shows ('what a successful classifieds platform looks like after twenty years of reasonable local decisions'); the Golf is explained as the professional-supply counterpart.
Lead-in says the table maps the eight problems to the chapters that pose and work them.

All 33 declared transitions are expressed at their boundaries, e.g. p02 emphasis ('Veldmark Group is fictional.'), p06 cause_effect ('That duplication comes from a history'), p11 contrast ('is the exception to'), p13 contrast ('Two caveats on reading it.'), p18 time ('When Ingrid arrives'), p20 problem_solution ('Veldmark's answer to these problems'), p27 similarity ('plays the same role'), p28 contrast ('Smaller stories'), conclusion conclusion_summary ('The three preface pages make one argument'), p33 cause_effect ('So'), and the hand-off to part-1. The logic gap in p33's second clause is recorded under flow_is_followable.

results.quote: The dated decisions the chapters rely on, by year (Figure 5's four plateaus):
results.finding: The lead-in frames the decision table by a figure the reader has not yet seen and by a 'by year' grouping the month-by-month table does not show; the plateau names appear only in Figure 5's caption after the table, so the reader had to read on and come back (flow-a item 8). Name the four plateaus in the lead-in or move Figure 5 before the table; also make the fragment a sentence.
results.corroborated_by: flow-b: item 1, forward Figure 5 reference and 'by year' label that doesn't match the table

results.quote: Single listings show the problems and the program's decisions best.
results.finding: The opener calls all five stories single listings, but the Barcelona ring is 180 listings from 26 accounts and the brown-out is a search incident; the reader paused over the mismatch (flow-a item 10). Reword so the opener covers listings, rings and incidents.
results.corroborated_by: flow-b: item 2, worked-examples opener doesn't fit two of the five examples

results.draft_locus: From the Preface to Part I ¶2
results.quote: So every chapter's opening scene is one more view of a group you already know, and each chapter explains a decision about a boundary, not a product choice.
results.finding: The second clause reads as a new claim slipped in under 'So' (flow-a item 13). The link exists in ¶1 ('it loses matches at its boundaries'; 'share platforms, not products') but the prose does not draw it; say that because the patterns are boundary failures and the program shares platforms beneath products, each chapter's decision is about a boundary.
results.corroborated_by: flow-b: item 4, the 'So' in the final hand-off doesn't follow

results.quote: so a fraud rule written on a Sunday night reaches Belgium on Wednesday and Poland and Portugal never
results.finding: The Copy-Paste Country bullet gives a specific incident nothing near it explains, and its only payoff ('a rule that reached Belgium three days late' in the bike paragraph) is far away and absent from the bike's table row, so the reader could not connect them (flow-a item 2). Either add the Belgium delay to the bike row or make the callout less specific.
results.corroborated_by: flow-b: item 7, Copy-Paste Country bullet gives more detail than a reader can place

results.quote: it sells for **€225** with a buyer fee of **€11.95**
results.finding: The bike is listed at €240 and the spine paragraph says 'Its chapters follow one €240 listing', but it sells for €225 with no word on why the price changed; both readers re-read to reconcile the figures (flow-a item 12). Add a few words (e.g. after a price agreed with the buyer).
results.corroborated_by: flow-b: item 3, unexplained price change in the bike example

results.quote: about **57 million** across the three marketplaces (31M + 14M + 12M; users of several brands are counted once per brand)
results.finding: The per-brand split appears before the brands are introduced, so it cannot be read, and it is repeated in the volumes table, which made the reader check whether the figures differed (flow-a item 3). Only flow-a reported it.

results.quote: Six months later, Femke's erasure request finds **seven** copies of the listing.
results.finding: Right after 'Their facts never change', the spine (and Golf) paragraphs add canonical facts not in the table, making the reader wonder whether the table is complete (flow-a item 11). Say the table gives the core facts. Only flow-a reported it.

Both readers describe the declared order (group described outside-in, then problems, program, worked examples, chapter use, hand-off), find every section's position clear and would not reorder any heading. Points both judged non-material and that the audience is expected to know (the introduction's general-manager scene, 'Ranking policy v1' left to its chapter, the Ghost Inventory teaser) are not counted.

results.quote: **Tradeyard Safe Deal** launches in the Netherlands.
results.finding: Safe Deal appears as a bare name in the history table and is first explained (in-platform payment) only in the brands section. Add a few words at first mention. Reported by flow-b only.

results.quote: Veldmark Ads is the exception to "four of everything"
results.finding: The phrase is quoted as if established, but in the body it is defined only later as problem 1 (the glance section says 'several times over'). Reported by flow-b only.

Other terms checked against the audience: liquidity and the liquidity metric are in already_knows (from the introduction); the failure-pattern names are in already_knows (from where-listing-systems-go-wrong); event contracts, strangler migration, entitlements and contact marketplace are within an experienced marketplace architect's vocabulary; 'the Yardstick monolith' in the key points is self-glossing and backed by 'a PHP monolith from 2006'; DSA, VIN, DMS, AVM and DVF are spelled out at first use. Paragraph openings start from given information.
The introduction states why one fictional group serves the book better than a toy or a real company, labels it fictional and gives a roadmap; none of the weak patterns.

The closing synthesizes the three preface pages, calls back to the general-manager scene and hands off to Part I; no 'in conclusion', no bare restatement, no body evidence. The boundary claim is prepared in ¶1 and in the spec's so_what; its weak connective is a flow point.

¶1 states what no section states (one argument at three sizes: liquidity machine, fifteen boundary failures, Veldmark's problems and Common Ground as the claim as a program); ¶2 gives the so-what (every scene is a view of a known group and a boundary decision) and the course of action for Part I.
Returns to the general-manager scene: 'the six minutes to searchable is Veldmark's problem 2, and the sold bike in Tuesday's alert e-mails is Femke's €240 city bike in 214 of them.'

The intro reader predicted all six roadmap items in order (glance and history; brands and volumes; systems and people; problems and Common Ground; worked examples and chapter use; closing on the preface), invented-but-consistent figures and tables as evidence, and a declarative briefing tone.

Reader named four problems with the expected patterns: Four of everything (Deal-Shaped Architecture), Six weeks for a category (Category Straitjacket, Attribute Junkyard), Duplicates at Hearthly (Seeing Double), Payment-link phishing (Fast Mail for Fraudsters), plus Overlap in Poland.
Reader confirmed €225 and Monday 8 March, corrected the fee to €11.95 (5% × €225 + €0.70) and the reservation to 14:02, matching expected.
